summary: This informational document describes an architecture based on a Path Computation Element (PCE) for MPLS and GMPLS networks. Computing constrained paths across large, multi-domain, multi-region or multi-layer networks is hard, so special computation components may cooperate. It describes building blocks rather than every component.

plainLanguage.summary: Planning a trip across many countries is hard for one traveler alone. This document says a special planner who knows every map can work out the route, and several planners can pass the question along.

questions: what is a path computation element
what is the difference between a pce and a pcc
why is pce needed for multi-domain mpls
subtitle: A blueprint for handing constrained path computation in MPLS and GMPLS networks to dedicated, cooperating Path Computation Elements.

tldr.problem: Computing constrained paths across large, multi-domain, multi-region or multi-layer networks is complex, and the router at the head of a path often cannot see the whole network.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Path Computation Element (PCE), an entity that computes a path from a network graph and constraints, and a Path Computation Client (PCC) that asks it. PCEs can sit inside routers or on separate servers, and several can cooperate.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational architecture, not a protocol. It lists building blocks and the areas that still need standardization, such as PCC-PCE communication and PCE discovery.

today: RFC 4655 is an Informational RFC published in August 2006, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes building blocks and leaves detailed protocols, discovery and MIB work to other documents.

sections.title: Introduction and Definitions
sections.content:
Constraint-based path computation is a fundamental building block for traffic engineering in MPLS and GMPLS networks. In large, multi-domain networks, path computation is complex and may need special computational components and cooperation between domains. A domain is any collection of network elements within a common sphere of address management or path computation responsibility, such as an IGP area or an Autonomous System.

A Path Computation Element (PCE) is an entity that computes a network path or route based on a network graph and applies computational constraints. It is an application that can sit within a network node or on an out-of-network server, and the RFC makes no assumption about how it is built. A PCC is any client application that requests a computation from a PCE. The PCE function is orthogonal to the forwarding capability of the node that hosts it.

The RFC separates single PCE path computation (one PCE handles a given path) from multiple PCE path computation (several PCEs share the work), and the centralized model (one PCE computes all paths in a domain) from the distributed model (the work is shared among PCEs). A PCE-based model is not exclusive and can be used alongside other path computation models.
sections.plainLanguage: A Path Computation Element is a helper that knows the map and finds a good route. A Path Computation Client is whoever asks it. The helper can live in your own device or somewhere else.

sections.title: Why a PCE Is Needed
sections.content:
Section 4 lists situations where a separate PCE helps, and says the list is illustrative rather than exhaustive.

  • CPU-intensive computation: placing a set of LSPs to optimize an objective, multi-criteria paths, or minimal-cost point-to-multipoint (Steiner) trees may be too heavy for some routers.
  • Partial visibility: an ingress router cannot see inside another domain, so loose routes cannot guarantee an optimal or even a viable path without trial and error.
  • Absence of the TED: maintaining the Traffic Engineering Database can drain a node's memory and CPU, or the IGP may lack TE extensions.
  • Node outside the routing domain: for example a customer-edge router, where computation at the ingress is not wanted.
  • No control plane or routing capability: legacy optical elements that have only data and management planes.
  • Backup paths and multi-layer networks: coordinated backup computation for bandwidth protection, and paths that cross client and server layers.
  • Path selection policy applied at the PCE.

The RFC also gives non-motivations. PCE is not intended for the whole Internet; it applies to a set of domains with known relationships, at a scale similar to peering between Service Providers. And a single centralized PCE cannot guarantee that a TE LSP will be established, since the network can still fail or contend for resources after computation.
sections.plainLanguage: A helper is useful when the map is too big for you, when you can only see your own country, or when your device is too small to do the math.

sections.title: The Basic PCE Configurations
sections.content:
Section 5 shows five ways to arrange PCEs.

  • Composite PCE node: a router that also implements the PCE. The routing protocol builds the TED, and the PCE operates on it, subject to local policy, to answer the node's own signaling engine.
  • External PCE: the head-end node sends a request to a separate PCE, which uses its own TED and returns a response.
  • Multiple PCE path computation: the returned path is partial or loose, so a downstream node consults another PCE for the next hops.
  • Multiple PCE path computation with inter-PCE communication: the first PCE asks other PCEs for help. This is not a distributed computation algorithm, but it lets distinct PCEs compute different segments. The PCC may see no difference from the external PCE case.
  • Management-based PCE usage: a network management system acts as the PCC and gives the head-end LSR a fully computed explicit path.

The RFC lists the areas that need standardization: PCC-PCE and PCE-PCE communication including policy information, routing and signaling extensions for PCE discovery and inter-domain paths, metrics to evaluate path computation models, and MIB modules.
sections.plainLanguage: The helper can live inside your device, in a separate box, or you can have a chain of helpers passing the question along, one per country. From your side you may not notice which design is used.

sections.title: Architectural Considerations
sections.content:
Section 6 covers the components and how they interact. PCE changes only how paths are computed, not how TE LSPs are signaled, maintained or torn down.

Discovery and selection: a PCC must know where a PCE is, through configuration or a discovery mechanism, and requests are targeted to a specific PCE, not broadcast. Where several PCEs are known, the PCC picks one under policy, using advertised capabilities such as supported constraints, computational capacity, switching layers, path selection criteria, whether the PCE is stateless or can send updates about better paths, whether it can compute point-to-multipoint trees, and whether it can ensure resource sharing between backup tunnels. Detecting PCE liveness is called mandatory.

Communication: a request/response protocol carries the source and destination, bandwidth and QoS parameters, resources and shared risk link groups to use or avoid, the number of disjoint paths, and policy information. A failure returns an error with as much information as possible, and possibly advice on which constraints to relax. The RFC makes no assumption that the PCC-PCE and PCE-PCE protocols are identical.

TED synchronization can come from the IGP, from out-of-band retrieval, or from non-IGP sources such as operator-configured link usage policies and TE LSP data. A PCE may hold only a partial TED. A stateful PCE also tracks existing paths and reserved resources, which can improve results but needs reliable synchronization; a stateless PCE treats each request independently.

Other topics include synchronized computation of several paths, confidentiality (a provider must not have to reveal its topology, so partial paths with loose hops must be possible), policy, unsolicited PCE updates, and crankback, where a failure is reported back to a domain boundary that tries another path.
sections.plainLanguage: You have to know which helper to ask, check that it is awake, and speak a language it understands. A helper that remembers every trip it has planned can plan better, but it has to keep a lot of notes and keep them up to date.

sections.title: Evaluation and Manageability
sections.content:
Section 8 lists metrics for judging PCE-based solutions, not for choosing paths: optimality, scalability, load sharing, multi-path computation, reoptimization, path computation time, network stability, TED synchronization accuracy and speed, handling of unsatisfiable requests, and policy. It notes that improving one, such as path optimality, is likely to affect another, such as computation time.

Section 9 covers manageability. It must be possible to enable and disable the PCE function, with a graceful shutdown so a PCE does not simply disappear but warns its PCCs and handles queued requests. Operations are expected to be modeled with MIB modules, including statistics and notifications, with care not to flood the network with SNMP notifications.

The architecture may increase TE LSP setup times and cause congestion if many requests arrive at once, most severely in busy networks and after failures. Operators should be able to rate limit requests, and a PCE should be able to report impending congestion to the operator and to its PCCs.
sections.plainLanguage: You need a way to grade the helpers and a way to switch them on and off safely, without flooding the network with alarm bells. If too many people ask at once, the system should slow the questions down.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
A PCE-based architecture must be judged by its effect on the security of the routing and signaling already in the network. Intra-domain use is less likely to be an issue, but more inter-domain information flow and easier inter-domain path setup may increase vulnerability. Multi-domain solutions MUST examine their confidentiality effects.

Using a PCE that is not co-resident with the PCC adds specific risks: interception of requests or responses, impersonation of a PCE or PCC, falsification of TE information, policy information or PCE capabilities, and denial-of-service attacks on a PCE or its communication. The RFC expects PCE solutions to address these with authentication and security techniques, and expects applicability statements to carry detailed security sections.
sections.plainLanguage: If a stranger could pretend to be your trip planner, or read your questions, you would be in trouble. So the helpers must prove who they are, and that work is left to later documents.
